Two factors and their numbers of levels

blocks.md: Without interactions, a regression assumes each explanation works the same way whatever the others are doing: an extra 100 square feet adds the same amount to a house's price in every neighbourhood. An interaction relaxes that. Multiplying living area by a neighbourhood indicator lets each extra square foot be worth more in one neighbourhood than in the other. Multiplying age by income lets the effect of getting older on pizza spending depend on how much a person earns. Multiplying two group indicators lets the wage gap for black women differ from the black gap plus the female gap added together.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: Interactions are how a regression answers "does the effect differ across groups or levels?", and reading their coefficients needs the case-by-case equations, not the table alone.
Three kinds, each read by writing out $E[y]$ for every case.
**Slope and intercept indicators** ($D$ a dummy, $x$ quantitative):

blocks.tex: E[y] = \beta_1 + \delta D + \beta_2 x + \gamma(x \times D) = \begin{cases}(\beta_1 + \delta) + (\beta_2 + \gamma)x, & D = 1\\ \beta_1 + \beta_2 x, & D = 0\end{cases}

blocks.md: **Two quantitative variables**: $E[y] = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x + \beta_3 w + \beta_4(x \times w)$ gives $\partial E[y]/\partial x = \beta_2 + \beta_4 w$.
**Houses in University Town** (price in \$1000s, $SQFT$ in 100s of square feet, 1,000 houses):

An extra 100 square feet adds \$7,664 elsewhere and $7.664 + 1.280 = 8.944$, \$8,944, in University Town. The location premium grows with size: for a 2,000-square-foot house ($SQFT = 20$) it is $28.12 + 1.280 \times 20 = 53.71$, about \$53,700.

blocks.md: **Pizza spending, age and income** (40 people, income in \$1000s):
The effect of a year of age is $-2.977 - 0.1232\,INCOME$: $-6.06$ dollars a year at an income of \$25,000 and $-14.07$ at \$90,000. Older people spend less on pizza, and more so the richer they are.

Holding education fixed: white women earn \$4.78 an hour less than white men ($\delta_2$); black women earn $-4.169 - 4.785 + 3.844 = -5.11$ less than white men ($\delta_1 + \delta_2 + \gamma$) and $-4.169 + 3.844 = -0.32$ less than white women ($\delta_1 + \gamma$). Whether race and gender matter at all is a joint test of $\delta_1 = \delta_2 = \gamma = 0$ ([F Test of Joint Hypotheses](note:f-test-of-joint-hypotheses)).

An effect plot draws one line per group: parallel lines mean no slope interaction; lines that cross or fan out show one. In the prestige data, letting education and log income interact with occupation type gives three different slopes.

blocks.md:
- **Reading the main effect as the effect.** With $x \times w$ in the model, $\beta_2$ is the effect of $x$ when $w = 0$, which may be outside the data (an income of zero).
- **Leaving out the main effects.** $y = \beta_1 + \beta_2 x + \gamma(x \times D)$ forces both groups through the same intercept; the lecture's slope-only model does this.
- **Adding gaps without the interaction.** The black-female gap is $\delta_1 + \delta_2 + \gamma$, not $\delta_1 + \delta_2$.
- **Collinearity.** $x$, $w$ and $x \times w$ are often highly correlated (the pizza regression's condition number is 18,900), so individual $t$ statistics are small even when the terms matter jointly.
